tracks.narration: Gram–Schmidt cleans up the columns of a matrix — what is left behind?
Take a matrix A. Read it column by column — these two columns are the vectors we will orthogonalise.
Step one: normalise a one. Divide by its length. That is q one — a unit vector pointing along a one.
Step two: subtract from a two the part that lies along q one. The residual is perpendicular to q one. Normalise it — that is q two.
Read off the matrix R. Down the diagonal sit the lengths r one one and r two two. Above the diagonal sits r one two — the projection coefficient. Zero below. R is upper triangular.
Q carries the geometry — orthonormal directions. R carries the bookkeeping — the lengths and the projections. Together they rebuild A.
